claim: The tulip crash of 1637 ruined the Dutch economy.

heard.who: Charles Mackay, Memoirs of Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds (1841), as quoted by History.com
heard.quote: Substantial merchants were reduced almost to beggary, and many a representative of a noble line saw the fortunes of his house ruined beyond redemption.

answer: Mostly not. When the market collapsed in February 1637 many buyers defaulted, and traders who had already paid were left in debt or bankrupted. But few people took part: Goldgar found about 350 traders, mostly merchants and craftsmen, not the wider population.

facts.text: When the tulip market collapsed in February 1637, many buyers defaulted on their promises to pay, and traders who had already paid were left in debt or bankrupted.

sources.title: There Never Was a Real Tulip Fever
sources.quote: More and more people defaulted on their agreement to buy the tulips at the prices they'd promised, and the traders who had already made their payments were left in debt or bankrupted.

sources.title: On this day in 1637: The tulip bubble bursts
sources.quote: and many buyers refused to abide by their obligations.

sources.quote: when buyers who promised to pay 100 or 1,000 guilders for a tulip refused to pay up.

facts.text: Few people took part in the tulip trade: Anne Goldgar's archival research identified about 350 traders, mostly merchants and craftsmen, not the wider population.

sources.quote: I only identified about 350 people who were involved in the trade

contested.text: Whether the tulip price rise was a speculative bubble. The economist Peter Garber argued that bulb prices moved as prices of rare bulbs do today, so no bubble need be assumed.

sources.title: Bubbles
sources.quote: Yet economist Peter Garber provided compelling evidence that "tulipmania" did not generate a bubble.
